source: Plain-language explanations of each ratio in engines/ratios.js: what it reads, why it matters, what moves it, and which household fields it looks at. Written for this app; the conventions quoted (28/36, 30% utilisation, 3-6 months, 4%) are the ones data/ratio_benchmarks.json cites.
confidenceNote: Explanations, not findings. 'Improve' says which direction the band calls healthier and what moves the figure; whether that is right for a particular life is the reader's call, and several bands are wrong for particular lives by design.
note: One entry per ratio id. `looksAt` lists shared/ownership.js field ids; a page renders each as a link to the room that owns it, which is how every term on a ratio links to the number it is reading. A ratio missing here is a test failure (test/run.js), so a new ratio must come with its explanation.

debtToIncome.what: Every required debt payment in a month, as a share of what you earn before tax that month.
debtToIncome.why: It is the first number a lender reads, and it says how much of each paycheque is already spoken for before you buy anything.
debtToIncome.improve: Lower it by clearing a balance outright (Debt Payoff shows which one ends a payment soonest) or by raising gross pay. Extra payments do not move it until an account closes.

housingRatio.what: Housing plus utilities, as a share of gross monthly income.
housingRatio.why: The 28% rule underwriters use. Above it, housing crowds out saving and every other line, whatever the rest looks like.
housingRatio.improve: Only two levers: a cheaper place, or more income. Housing Decision compares rent against buying on the same footing.

backEndRatio.what: Housing plus every other debt payment, as a share of gross monthly income.
backEndRatio.why: The 36% rule, and the 43% ceiling for a qualified mortgage. It is the number that decides whether a lender says yes.
backEndRatio.improve: Clear the smallest payment that is not the mortgage; each closed account drops the ratio by its whole payment.

savingsRate.what: What is left of gross pay after a year of spending and an estimate of tax, as a share of gross.
savingsRate.why: The single number that sets how many years to financial independence. Twice the rate is roughly half the time.
savingsRate.improve: Raise it from either side: spend less on the biggest lines (Cash Flow), or capture the employer match and automate the rest (Savings Rate).

emergencyFundMonths.what: Cash and savings divided by a month of spending: how many months the cash alone would carry you.
emergencyFundMonths.why: It is the cushion between a surprise and a credit card. Three to six months is the convention; Runway tests it against your own worst month.
emergencyFundMonths.improve: Build cash first, before extra debt payments or investing, until it reaches the months you chose in Sleep At Night.

creditUtilization.what: Card balances as a share of the credit limits on those cards.
creditUtilization.why: Scoring models are believed to read anything above 30% as strain, and under 10% as excellent. It moves a credit score faster than almost anything else.
creditUtilization.improve: Pay a card down below 30% of its limit before its statement date, or ask for a higher limit and leave it unused.

netWorthToIncome.what: Net worth divided by a year of gross income.
netWorthToIncome.why: It says how many years of pay you have turned into wealth. The useful benchmark is by age, which is the retirement multiple below.
netWorthToIncome.improve: Anything that grows net worth: saving more, paying debt down, or letting investments compound.

liquidityRatio.what: Everything you could turn into cash quickly, divided by a month of spending.
liquidityRatio.why: A wider net than the emergency fund: it counts a brokerage account too. It is how long you could go before selling anything hard to sell.
liquidityRatio.improve: Mark which assets are liquid on The Statement, and hold the emergency fund in cash rather than in things that take weeks to sell.

solvencyRatio.what: Net worth as a share of everything you own.
solvencyRatio.why: Below zero, you owe more than you have. It says how much of what you own is actually yours.
solvencyRatio.improve: Pay debt down; every dollar of principal cleared raises it. Adding an asset bought with a loan does not.

currentRatio.what: Liquid assets divided by a year of required debt payments.
currentRatio.why: Under 1×, a year of minimums is more than you could lay hands on. It is a stress test for a bad year.
currentRatio.improve: Grow cash or clear a payment. Either side moves it.

retirementMultiple.what: Investments as a multiple of gross income, against a benchmark for your age.
retirementMultiple.why: The common milestones: one year of pay by 30, three by 40, six by 50. It says whether retirement saving is on pace for your age.
retirementMultiple.improve: Raise the contribution rate; the FIRE room shows what one more percent does over the years left.

lifeInsuranceMultiple.what: Life cover as a multiple of gross income, against a ten-times rule of thumb.
lifeInsuranceMultiple.why: If people depend on your income, the cover replaces it. Ten times income is a convention, not a finding.
lifeInsuranceMultiple.improve: Enter your term life cover in Sleep At Night; the Coverage Checkup reads it against what it would have to carry.

carPaymentToIncome.what: Car loan payments as a share of gross monthly income.
carPaymentToIncome.why: The 10 to 15% guidance. A car payment is the commonest way a good income ends up with nothing left.
carPaymentToIncome.improve: Keep the car longer, or refinance a high-rate loan. Debt Payoff shows what an extra payment does to the term.

investedShare.what: Investments as a share of everything you own. It cannot exceed 100%.
investedShare.why: It says how much of what you own is working, against how much sits in cash, a car, or a home. Right for a renter, different for a homeowner.
investedShare.improve: Move cash beyond the cushion into investments; Sleep At Night says how much cushion that is.

fiRatio.what: What investments would pay at your safe withdrawal rate, as a share of a year of spending.
fiRatio.why: At 1.0 the portfolio covers the year and work is optional. It is FIRE progress in one number.
fiRatio.improve: Both levers: more invested, or less spending. A dollar less of yearly spending needs 25 dollars less invested.

debtToAsset.what: Total debt as a share of everything you own.
debtToAsset.why: Above 1 you are insolvent on paper. It is the balance-sheet view of how leveraged the household is.
debtToAsset.improve: Pay principal down, or let assets grow. Borrowing to buy an asset leaves it roughly unchanged.

personalCashFlowRatio.what: Take-home pay less everything that goes out, as a share of gross income.
personalCashFlowRatio.why: It is the margin the month runs on. Under 5% one surprise is a debt.
personalCashFlowRatio.improve: Cash Flow shows every line; the biggest ones move it most.

ruleOf72.what: 72 divided by the expected return, in percent: roughly how many years money takes to double.
ruleOf72.why: A shortcut for feeling compounding. At 7% money doubles every ten years, so a dollar at 25 is eight at 55.
ruleOf72.improve: Not a thing to improve. The expected return is an assumption in the FIRE room.

safeWithdrawalRate.what: The share of investments drawn each year that a portfolio is assumed to sustain.
safeWithdrawalRate.why: It sets the FI number: a year of spending divided by this rate. 4% is the convention from the Trinity study.
safeWithdrawalRate.improve: It is an assumption, adjustable in the FIRE room, not a figure about you.

loanToValue.what: Mortgage balance as a share of the property's value.
loanToValue.why: Under 80% mortgage insurance usually drops off; over 95% there is no equity to fall back on.
loanToValue.improve: Principal payments and time. Housing Decision reads the property value from The Statement.

homeEquityRatio.what: Property value less the mortgage, as a share of the property value.
homeEquityRatio.why: The mirror of loan-to-value: how much of the house is yours.
homeEquityRatio.improve: Pay principal down; a rising market does the rest, or the reverse.

debtPayoffVelocity.what: A year of debt payments as a share of total debt, before interest.
debtPayoffVelocity.why: It says how fast the minimums alone would clear what you owe. A low figure means the balance is mostly interest.
debtPayoffVelocity.improve: Extra payments toward the highest rate; Debt Payoff shows the months saved.

burnRateCents.why: Every runway number divides cash by this. It is the number to know before any other.
burnRateCents.improve: Cash Flow, line by line. The fixed lines are the floor; everything above it is cuttable.

runwayMonths.what: Cash divided by monthly spending: the months the cash lasts with nothing coming in.
runwayMonths.why: The same arithmetic as the emergency fund, named the way people ask for it between jobs.
runwayMonths.improve: More cash, or a lower floor. Runway shows the months at the floor rather than at today's spending.

liquidToIlliquid.what: Liquid assets divided by everything else you own.
liquidToIlliquid.why: It says whether wealth is reachable or locked in a house and a retirement account. There is no right number.
liquidToIlliquid.improve: Rate each asset's liquidity on The Statement so the figure reads what you actually hold.

cashDrag.what: Cash as a share of everything you own.
cashDrag.why: Cash beyond the cushion earns less than inflation. Whether it is too much depends entirely on why it is there.
cashDrag.improve: Decide the cushion in Sleep At Night; invest what sits above it.

revolvingShare.what: Card balances as a share of total debt.
revolvingShare.why: Card debt is the expensive kind. A high share says the debt is costing the most it can.
revolvingShare.improve: Clear cards first, whatever the strategy. Debt Payoff shows the interest each order costs.

needsToWants.what: Essential spending divided by discretionary spending.
needsToWants.why: A split, not a score. It shows how much of the month is choice and how much is obligation.
needsToWants.improve: Nothing to fix by itself. The 50/30/20 split in Cash Flow is one convention to read it against.

discretionaryIncomeRatio.what: Discretionary spending as a share of gross monthly income.
discretionaryIncomeRatio.why: The room to cut if a month goes wrong, and the room to enjoy if it does not.
discretionaryIncomeRatio.improve: The Rerank ranks each line by what it gives you against what it costs.

realEstateConcentration.what: Property value as a share of everything you own.
realEstateConcentration.why: Normal to be high for a homeowner. It says how much of your wealth is one building in one place.
realEstateConcentration.improve: Grow the other assets around it; there is no reason to sell a home you want.

incomeConcentration.what: The largest income source as a share of household income.
incomeConcentration.why: One paycheque reads 100%. It is how much of the household's income one employer decides.
incomeConcentration.improve: A second earner, a side income, or an income-producing asset each lower it. Side Hustle prices the second.

confidenceWeightedNetWorth.what: Each asset weighted by how sure its value is, less debts.
confidenceWeightedNetWorth.why: A brokerage balance is certain; a private business or a collectible is not. This is the net worth you could count on.
confidenceWeightedNetWorth.improve: Rate each asset's confidence on The Statement; nothing else moves it honestly.

liquidityLadder.what: Assets reachable within a year as a share of all assets.
liquidityLadder.why: The four rungs: today, this month, this year, not without a penalty. It is the answer to 'how much could I actually get at'.
liquidityLadder.improve: Rate each asset's liquidity on The Statement, and keep the emergency fund on the top rung.

shadowRunway.what: Cash plus Roth contributions plus home equity at a haircut, divided by monthly spending.
shadowRunway.why: The runway if you were willing to raid the Roth and sell the house. Longer than the plain runway, and it costs more to use.
shadowRunway.improve: The same as runway: cash first. Roth basis is read from The Statement.

worstPlausibleYearCoverage.what: Cash divided by a year in which everything goes wrong at once: job loss, the deductible, the essentials, net of the benefit.
worstPlausibleYearCoverage.why: 1× means the cash would carry that year. It replaces the vague 3 to 6 months once the inputs exist.
worstPlausibleYearCoverage.improve: Cash, a lower deductible, or a lower floor of essentials. Sleep At Night shows the pieces.

automationRatio.what: Savings that happen without you, as a share of all savings.
automationRatio.why: Automated saving is the saving that actually happens. What you have to remember to do, you sometimes do not.
automationRatio.improve: The Skill Stacker asks which contributions run on their own; set up the ones that do not.

givingRate.what: Gifts as a share of take-home pay, monthly.
givingRate.why: A figure, not a score: the tithe is a religious convention, not a financial one.
givingRate.improve: Giving sets a target and shows what a percentage of take-home is in dollars.

netWorthInYears.what: Net worth divided by a year of spending.
netWorthInYears.why: How long what you own would last at what you spend, before growth. It reads like the FI ratio, in years.
netWorthInYears.improve: Both levers: a higher net worth, or a lower year of spending.

humanToFinancialCapital.what: The present value of your pay to the stop age, divided by cash plus investments.
humanToFinancialCapital.why: High early in a career, falling toward zero as pay becomes assets. It says how much of your wealth is still in the future.
humanToFinancialCapital.improve: It falls on its own as you save. Protecting the income, with disability and life cover, is the point while it is high.

bracketRoom.what: The top of the current federal bracket less taxable income.
bracketRoom.why: How much more you could earn or convert before the next dollar is taxed higher. A planning figure for Roth conversions and raises.
bracketRoom.improve: Not a thing to improve; Tax shows what a conversion inside the room costs.

bridgeGapYears.what: Years between the age FI arrives and 59½, when retirement accounts open.
bridgeGapYears.why: Those years have to be funded from taxable money and Roth basis. Zero means no bridge is needed.
bridgeGapYears.improve: Save the bridge years in taxable accounts; The Statement shows what is reachable before 59½.

lifestyleInflation.what: The rise in yearly spending divided by the rise in income since a snapshot a year ago.
lifestyleInflation.why: Below 50% most of a raise was kept. Above 100% spending rose faster than pay. Needs time to exist before it can say anything.
lifestyleInflation.improve: Freeze a snapshot now; when the next raise lands, put half of it somewhere automatic before the month absorbs it.

netWorthGrowthRate.what: Net worth now against a year ago, annualised.
netWorthGrowthRate.why: Progress in one number. It is what a snapshot is for.
netWorthGrowthRate.improve: Freeze today's numbers, then again in a year. History draws the line between them.

withdrawalRate.what: Spending not covered by income, as a share of investments, each year.
withdrawalRate.why: The number a retiree lives by. Under 4% is the convention that lasts thirty years; over 5% is the watch line.
withdrawalRate.improve: Less drawn, more income, or a larger portfolio. Decumulation shows how long the money lasts at each.

fiDate.what: Today plus the years to FI at the current pace.
fiDate.why: The same projection as the FI year on the dashboard, to the month. It is the date the savings rate is buying.
fiDate.improve: The savings rate moves it more than anything. The lens on every page reads a dollar as days off this date.
